item.title: Single feathers may reveal whether eastern black rails stay in Texas or migrate north
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Single feathers may reveal whether eastern black rails stay in Texas or migrate north

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

High-stepping like you're in a marching band while dragging a rope through a wetland at night can make you wonder about your life choices. Several plastic bottles, each filled with two or three noisy cat toys, are attached to the rope. It's pitch black, and all I can hear are the cat toys jingling, the mosquitoes buzzing in my ears and the wetland grasses bouncing in the wind.

I'm out with several of my graduate students, searching for a little bird that at first glance may look like a mouse running along the ground, since this bird doesn't like to fly.

"Rail! Rail!" yells out one of my grad students, and we stop pulling the rope to carefully approach the place where she saw the bird land after it flew a short distance away from the commotion. There it is, a black rail, sitting on the grass watching us as we slowly lower a dip net over it. A moment later, the bird is in the net. We have successfully caught an eastern black rail!

We're out in the wetlands of coastal Texas to catch these federally threatened birds. We are studying what wetlands they prefer and will take feather samples to understand their migratory patterns. Eastern black rails are sparrow-sized marsh birds that live in coastal wetlands along the Gulf and Atlantic coasts and in small inland populations, mostly in Colorado and Kansas. These cute little rails spend most of their time on the ground hunting for invertebrates and seeds to eat and using the vegetation to protect themselves from predators and the hot Gulf Coast summer sun.

I place a small metal band on the bird's leg. This tag is engraved with a unique number that will allow us to identify this individual if we ever catch him again. I take a few measurements and some standardized photographs and carefully remove a single feather. The feather will be used to determine if this bird is a year-round resident of the Texas coast or just here for the winter before it migrates north again, probably to Colorado or Kansas.

Every time I hold a bird—especially one so special—I am simultaneously focused on its health and safety and on the magic of holding it. The bird is so small that I can wrap my hand all the way around it. I can feel its chest expanding and contracting as it breathes. Its red eye watches me as I measure its legs and wings. Once I verify that we have collected all the data, it's time to let this bird go back to its normal night routine.

I walk a short distance behind the dragline, crouch down and set the bird down on the ground with my dim headlamp shining on it. The rail pauses, looks around and then zip. It runs off into the grass: here one second, gone the next.

We carefully pick up all our gear and pack it back in our backpacks, making sure we haven't left anything behind. We grab the rope and keep on going, hoping to find another rail in this plot. We'll be out here several hours tonight and for the next two weeks as part of our larger project seeking to understand the impacts of fire on wetland systems and these tiny, threatened birds.

item.title: The avian champions of long-distance migration keep surprising scientists
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

The avian champions of long-distance migration keep surprising scientists

Swati Mestri

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

"The whole story began with an extinct bird from Hispaniola," said Min Zhao, a former postdoctoral associate at the Florida Museum of Natural History (now a postdoctoral researcher at Uppsala University).

The bird in question was identified as a woodcock in 2015 based on several fossils excavated by Florida Museum researchers in 1984 from a Haitian cave on the island of Hispaniola.

Woodcocks are medium-sized birds with long, slightly curved beaks that appear to protrude from their necks and a bouncy back-and-forth gait that looks like a funky, two-step dance number. Scientists think this comic method of locomotion may mimic the vibrations made by falling rain, which is a cue for earthworms to move upward before the soil becomes waterlogged and they drown. Instead, vertically migrating earthworms encounter the slender bill of the woodcock.

In a new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Florida Museum researchers sequenced ancient DNA from the fossil specimens and showed that what was thought to be a woodcock is actually a snipe.

That in itself isn't very surprising. Woodcocks and snipes are each other's closest relatives, having diverged from a common ancestor about 25 million years ago. To the untrained eye, they can look nearly identical. The misidentified snipe also had short wings and big legs—two common traits in island birds—compared with what scientists now know are its closest relatives.

Long-distance migrants that settled on islands

But the combined efforts of the research group reveal a broader story about migration and evolution in a group of birds famous for flying nonstop from the high latitudes of one hemisphere to those of the other.

"Shorebirds are the ultimate long-distance migrants," said study coauthor David Steadman, the emeritus curator of ornithology at the Florida Museum. "It's common for shorebirds to nest up in the Arctic tundra and winter in South America. There was recently a bristle-thighed curlew that was radio-tagged and showed up in New Zealand after flying 10,000 km (6,200 miles) without stopping."

Like curlews, woodcocks and snipes also travel long distances, but unlike curlews and most other shorebirds, they also include several species whose ancestors opted out of migration and permanently settled down on islands. There are eight living species of woodcock, for example, and six of them are endemic to islands.

"Some people argue that it's their migratory propensity that has led them to colonize islands. But there are a lot of migrant shorebirds that travel long distances. Woodcocks and snipes are the only ones setting up resident populations on islands. They've radiated on islands in the Caribbean, Japan, Indonesia, the western Pacific and the greater New Zealand area," Steadman said.

Reconstructing a family tree from museum specimens

Intrigued by the results of the ancient DNA analysis, Steadman and his colleagues wanted to see if they could learn more about how woodcocks and snipes evolved and radiated around the world over the last quarter-million years.

The study's coauthors collected small tissue samples from specimens in museums across the country for all but one of the 29 extant woodcock and snipe species. Jessica Oswald, a postdoctoral researcher then working at the Florida Museum of Natural History, extracted and sequenced DNA from these samples and—with help from coauthor Brian Stucky—managed to do so for the Hispaniolan fossils as well. She also included DNA from one additional extinct species, the South Island snipe, which disappeared in 1964 following the human-mediated introduction of black rats to South and Stewart islands in New Zealand.

They added the ages of shorebird fossils to their DNA data and analyzed both together to produce a time-calibrated phylogeny, or what is essentially the species-level equivalent of a family tree with dates added to it.

Several of the authors have conducted similar studies in the past. Coauthor Oswald extracted ancient DNA from numerous fossil specimens while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum.

Over the last several years, she and her colleagues have shown that large rodents called hutias were intentionally transported to the Bahamas by humans more than 1,000 years ago to be a source of food, and that an old folktale about a shipwrecked Spanish galleon and its equine passengers said to have been marooned on an island off the coast of Virginia is likely more fact than fiction.

They have also shown that Haitian cave rails—an extinct group of birds that once inhabited parts of the Caribbean—were most closely related to adzebills in New Zealand and flufftails in Africa and the South Pacific, not to species of rail living on the American continents.

They have shown that Caribbean parrots thought to be naturally endemic to certain islands are actually the last remnants of species that were once more broadly distributed before the arrival of humans in the area, and that an endangered dove endemic to Cuba is more genetically distinct than the now-extinct dodo—also in the dove family—and is likewise in danger of dying out.

Unexpected ocean crossings connect distant snipes

The results of the current study have a similar flavor to the revelation that Caribbean cave rails originally hailed from halfway around the world.

The first big mix-up occurred around 20 million years ago, when one or a few adventurous woodcocks made their way from Eurasia—where their relatives originated—to North America. At around the same time, snipes in Eurasia dispersed to South America, where they evolved into several species. These include the extinct Caribbean snipe whose ambiguous fossils would later vex ornithologists.…

item.title: Repeated bending strengthens sugar-based hydrogel instead of wearing it down
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Repeated bending strengthens sugar-based hydrogel instead of wearing it down

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

Most materials get weaker with use. But a team led by Chenfeng Ke, a professor of chemistry in Arts & Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis, has created a polymer that defies the usual laws of wear and tear.

"Our smart material actually gets stronger the more it's bent and strained," Ke said. "It has properties we have never seen before. It can remember, adapt, learn and grow. We're excited to think about the possible applications."

The breakthrough was described in a study published online in Nature Materials. Co-authors include graduate students Yufei Chen and Mingliang Bai and postdoctoral researcher Dan Zheng.

The patented polymer, created in Ke's lab with compatibility for 3D printing, is made from a biodegradable blend of sugar crystals and polyethylene glycol, a compound often used in laxatives and other health products. The mixture forms a hydrogel, a flexible material that can absorb and retain large amounts of water.

In tests, Ke and his team applied the material to a flexible, knee-like joint. "We bent it 10,000 times, and the material performed just as we predicted," Ke said. "The polymers in the hydrogel become more uniform and organized, making it stronger in exactly the places where the strain is happening."

The smart material owes its strength and adaptability to cyclodextrin, a sugar-based compound that forms ring-shaped structures. When the polymer is stretched or bent, these rings slide into position to reinforce the areas under strain. "These moving rings are critical to the structural design," Ke said.

In many ways, the material mimics biological materials in the human body, including collagen, a protein that gives skin its strength and elasticity. "Some of the most impressive smart materials are found in biology," Ke said. "We used nature for inspiration."

Ke believes the polymer could have medical applications, particularly in protecting and repairing tissues.

"Because it's made of sugar and polyethylene glycol, it's completely compatible with biological tissues," Ke said. "We expect this material to attract interest from surgeons or orthopedic medical device companies who are looking for new approaches."

For example, the material could be used to support artificial joints or to repair damaged tissues. In either case, areas that aren't subjected to stress or strain would remain soft and pliable. "If you're putting material into a body, you don't necessarily want it to be completely rigid," Ke said. "The material gets stronger only where it's needed."

Ke is a chemist, not an orthopedist or medical device specialist, and he acknowledges that other experts may recognize applications he has yet to consider.

"We want to work with experts at WashU Medicine and elsewhere to explore the possibilities," Ke said. "Hopefully this paper will help us get the word out to researchers and potential investors."

So far, Ke and his team have produced the material in small quantities, just tens of grams at a time. But with the concept successfully demonstrated, they believe production could scale up to meet demand.

The new polymer builds on Ke's broader research into creating innovative materials inspired by nature. In April 2025, he proposed a new generation of smart fabrics at A&S Innovates, Arts & Sciences' inaugural research pitch competition.

"We've shown it's possible to produce smart materials with a 3D printer and the right chemistry," Ke said. "We see a lot of possibilities."

Publication details

Dan Zheng et al., Mechanical adaptation drives out-of-equilibrium network reorganization and self-strengthening in adapt-ring networks, Nature Materials (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41563-026-02795-0

Journal information: Nature Materials

item.title: BepiColombo Arrives at Mercury
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Research & Developments is a blog for brief updates that provide context for the flurry of news that impacts science and scientists today.

After an eight-year journey, the BepiColombo mission has entered orbit around Mercury, where it will settle in for at least a year of science observations.

“Mercury is a challenging destination,” Santa Martinez, the European Space Agency’s (ESA) mission manager for BepiColombo, said during a 31 August press event. “What makes this mission really unique is that for the first time in space exploration, we are bringing two spacecraft to the vicinity of the planet, and we are going to put them in orbit around this mysterious body.”

BepiColombo is only the third mission to visit Mercury. NASA’s Mariner 10 flew by Mercury in 1973 and NASA’s MESSENGER mission orbited the planet from 2011–2015. BepiColombo is a joint mission from ESA and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).

The mission is made up of two orbiters: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) from ESA and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio) from JAXA. Both orbiters were carried to Mercury by the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) and are protected by a sun shield.

MTM separated from the orbiters on 3 September. The still-connected MPO-Mio entered Mercury’s orbit today.

MPO’s mission is to map Mercury’s heavily-cratered surface and catalog its surface geology. Spectrometers focusing on several wavelengths will create maps of the planet’s surface composition and temperature, an altimeter will map surface topography, an accelerometer and gravitometer will map the planet’s gravitational field, and a radio science experiment will determine the size of the planet’s core. Another instrument will study Mercury’s exosphere and its interactions with solar plasma.

Mio will map Mercury’s magnetosphere, magnetic field, and plasma environment. Mercury has a magnetic field but scientists don’t understand what sustains it or why it is offset from the planet’s center. Mio is designed to help answer these questions, study how the magnetic field changes over time, and observe how the planet magnetically interacts with its closest neighbor, the Sun.

An Arduous Journey

BepiColombo launched in 2018 and completed several flybys of Earth, Venus, and Mercury as it fought against the Sun’s gravity on its journey to the inner solar system. Each flyby provided valuable scientific data that the team is still exploring.

“Reaching Mercury is actually harder than reaching Pluto,” Azul Pinochet-Barros, editor for operations activities at ESA’s European Space Operations Centre, said during the 3 September livestream of MTM’s separation from the propulsion module. “The challenge isn’t getting closer to the Sun. It’s losing enough energy to match Mercury’s path around the Sun. This makes Mercury the least explored planet in the inner solar system.”

Each of the nine planetary flybys was critical for shedding some of the spacecraft’s momentum as it spiraled inward toward Mercury. In 2024, a glitch in the mission’s thrusters prevented them from operating at full power, which necessitated an adjustment in the craft’s trajectory and a delay in BepiColombo’s arrival at Mercury from December 2025 to November 2026.

The next step in the mission will happen on 9–10 December when MPO and Mio will separate and enter individual polar orbits around Mercury. Science operations will begin in April 2027. The nominal mission will last a year, with a planned extended mission through 2029.

“This is going to bring to humanity and to the scientific community unprecedented views of the Mercury planet, and it’s going to open a new chapter in our understanding of the solar system,” Martinez said.

—Kimberly M. S. Cartier (@astrokimcartier.bsky.social), Staff Writer

item.title: Oceans and Forests Have Absorbed Roughly Half Our Carbon Emissions for Decades, Slowing Climate Change. But Can They Keep It Up?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels, raising global temperatures in the process.

Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.

The world’s oceans have absorbed 35% of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.

The importance of these two enormous natural carbon sinks cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.

If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their remaining carbon budgets – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.

But what if those carbon sinks change?

We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an alternative method for measuring these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.

We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that expansion might begin to slow down, leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.

The Fiendishly Difficult Task of Measuring Carbon Sinks

Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.

Computer models can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. Satellites can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.

As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.

Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen (O₂), combined with atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements, to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks take up carbon dioxide.

This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.

This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.

What We Found

When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.

In contrast to most computer model simulations, we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than predicted by most models, and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.

Where Is the Climate Headed?

If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.

For example, warmer waters are not able to hold as much gas, such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at mixing into the deep ocean, which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years.

The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.

Carbon Cycle Models Need to Improve

For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.

Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.

Looking Ahead

We believe our study improves understanding of global carbon sinks and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.

The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. Calibrating the measurements is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they expel some oxygen into the atmosphere. We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. And to take into account variability in ocean circulation and other ocean processes, we have to average our results over 10-year time frames.…

item.title: 'Like walking the plank': For 3,000 years, Indigenous people herded bison off a unique cliff in Texas, study reveals
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

'Like walking the plank': For 3,000 years, Indigenous people herded bison off a unique cliff in Texas, study reveals

At a cliff site in Texas, archaeologists discovered hundreds of bison bones, stone tools and arrowheads, suggesting Indigenous people used "bison jumps" to hunt.

Archaeologists have uncovered an extremely rare example of a "bison jump" in the Texas Panhandle, where a natural geological formation allowed Indigenous people to hunt North America's largest living land mammal for 3,000 years. The discovery confirms that the prehistoric hunting technique — which involved channeling a herd of bison into a stampede off a cliff, akin to "walking the plank" — was not limited to the northern Plains like experts previously thought.

"Bison jumping is an iconic, uniquely North American hunting technique that yielded some of the most productive food-getting events in the history of human hunting," researchers wrote in a study published online Nov. 9 in the journal American Antiquity.

Although jump sites are well known throughout the northern Plains, only one such site had ever been found in the southern Plains. But a second bison jump called Nighthawk has now been identified in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle, and researchers found that Indigenous people used the Nighthawk bison jump for millennia.

"Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility," study first author Gus Costa, an archaeologist at Rice University in Houston, said in a statement.

Nighthawk was found when bison remains began eroding from a bone bed (a place where bones naturally accumulate) underneath a roughly 65-foot-tall (20 meters) cliff spur. Archaeologists investigated and found chipped stone tools near the bones, as well as a few arrowheads. Several of the bison bones had cut marks from stone tools consistent with prehistoric butchery practices. These discoveries added up to a possible bison jump.

"The only way bison can arrive at the site is by falling from above, as the site surface is sandwiched between two cliffs," the researchers wrote. Indigenous hunters likely used the cliff's natural spur shape to herd the bison to their deaths. "Instead of a stampede toward a surprise fall, Nighthawk could have operated more like 'walking the plank,'" according to the researchers.

Even more surprising than the discovery of a bison jump site in the southern Plains was the length of time the jump was used.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A series of radiocarbon dates revealed that there were at least seven mass bison kills at Nighthawk over a span of three millennia, between roughly 1550 B.C. and A.D. 1550. One of these events, which the researcher named Kill 3, was responsible for most of the bison bones. That enormously successful hunt most likely took place around A.D. 300 to 400 and would have required an immense labor force and precise coordination.

"Bison jumping is a complicated community effort," Costa said. "Large scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful."

- The ancestors of today's Indigenous people arrived in the Americas during the coldest part of the last ice age, study suggests

- Ancient Indigenous people in New Mexico lived through extreme climate change 23,000 years ago, study suggests

- DNA study of nearly 200 Indigenous genomes reveals unknown Asian 'ghost' population contributed to American ancestry

It is not entirely clear what the Indigenous hunters were doing with the bison killed in the hunt. In the northern Plains, archaeologists have long assumed that bison jumps were generally performed in the fall and used to provision the community for winter. Bison in the North were used to make pemmican, a shelf-stable mix of dried meat and rendered fat.

But although pemmican was an extremely useful foodstuff and trade good in the North, it was likely too warm in Texas for bison fat to last more than a few weeks, the researchers wrote. This may mean that the southern Plains bison hunts were more useful for displaying power and building alliances.

All of the kill events at Nighthawk were at least a century apart, with an average of 500 years between each bison jump. That points to an infrequent use of the jump but also a clear memory of its utility.

"The simplest explanation for long-lived jump facilities is that these techniques were passed down over long time spans rather than revived again and again," the researchers wrote.

Costa, A. G., Houk, B. A., Lyle, A. S., Bement, L., Lintz, C., Lawrence, K. L., Frederick, C. D., & Culleton, B. J. (2026). The Nighthawk bison jump: New evidence for recurrent Late Holocene bison jumping in the Southern Plains. American Antiquity, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1017/aaq.2026.10229

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

item.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

- Date:

- November 21, 2026

- Source:

- York University

- Summary:

- AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.

- Share:

Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.

But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."

A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI

The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.

The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.

AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story

The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.

The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.

That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.

Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior

The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.

If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.…

item.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

- Date:

- November 21, 2026

- Source:

- Kyushu University

- Summary:

- Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

- Share:

We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time

Now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times."

Atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A New Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times

The researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

"It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a new technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times."

That improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A New Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity

The findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening new possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

For now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

"Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the big next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics."

If successful, such experiments could offer scientists a new way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.
